name: adapter
intent: Present an existing component through the exact target contract its client already consumes, translating calls, results and boundary semantics without adding responsibilities or pretending a missing capability exists.
problem: An existing or foreign component has useful behaviour but speaks a different protocol: method names and signatures, data shapes, units, lifecycle, error model or sync/async contract do not satisfy the target. If every caller performs ad hoc conversion, semantics drift, vendor types leak and provider replacement becomes a cross-cutting rewrite; changing the adaptee or target may be impossible or too disruptive.
context: Integration work where one side is outside your control: legacy modules, vendor SDKs, generated clients, foreign data formats or units, and the ports-and-adapters boundary of a hexagonal architecture. Applies in statically typed languages - where an adapter class is also the compile-time proof that the required interface is satisfied - and in structurally or dynamically typed ones, where a thin wrapper usually replaces a declared target interface.
benefits: The client depends on the interface it wants: translation lives in one class instead of being repeated at every call site.
Neither side changes: the adaptee stays untouched (essential for vendor, legacy and shared code) and the client keeps its stable contract.
Swappability: replacing a vendor, upgrading an SDK or adding a second provider costs one new adapter, not a refactor of the callers.
Testability: the target interface is a seam - an in-memory or fake adapter substitutes for the real dependency in tests.
Change is localised: when the adaptee's API drifts or its version is bumped, the blast radius is one small, reviewable class.
The mismatch becomes explicit and documented: units, encodings, nullability, parameter order and error taxonomies get a named translation instead of folklore.
tradeoffs: One extra type and one delegation hop per call - negligible at a boundary, measurable inside hot loops or for high-frequency short-lived objects.

It adapts the interface, not the semantics: units, error meanings, ordering, null handling, timeouts and idempotency must be translated deliberately, and a name-only adapter silently produces plausible wrong behaviour.
The adapter becomes a compatibility surface that must track the adaptee's API drift; every upgrade is an opportunity for a quiet translation bug.

Object adapters hold a reference, so ownership and lifetime must be decided (who closes it, shared or owned, listener and descriptor leaks); class adapters freeze the concrete adaptee and fail on sealed/final types and adaptee subclasses.

In structural or dynamically typed languages nothing proves the adapter is needed or correct: an adaptee may accidentally satisfy the shape, and an adapter can drift out of sync with the target without a compiler complaint.
Adapter chains and two-way adapters multiply indirection and obscure stack traces; an adapter that grows business logic stops being an adapter.
Adapter, Decorator, Proxy and Facade share one wrapper shape, so misuse (mislabelling one intent as another) muddies the design and the review discussion.

participants.responsibility: The interface the client is written against - abstract class, interface, protocol, trait or a documented duck-typed shape. It defines the operations and the contract (including errors and null semantics) the adapter must honour.
Code that collaborates only with Target; it does not know whether a concrete type or an adapter stands behind the interface, nor which adaptee is wrapped.
The existing class with useful behaviour but an incompatible interface. It is never modified and remains unaware that an adapter exists.
Implements Target by delegating to an adaptee instance, translating names, argument and return shapes, units, nullability and errors along the way. It owns the translation and nothing else.
Chooses which adapter to instantiate for a configured provider, protocol or service id, so the selection of an adaptee stays out of the client.

use_cases: Wrapping a third-party or vendor SDK behind your own interface so business code never imports vendor types.
Modernising a legacy module incrementally: new code talks to the target interface while the old component is adapted in place.
Supporting several interchangeable providers (payments, storage, messaging, analytics) through one internal contract, with one adapter each.
Adapting a callback- or error-first API to promises/async or to an observer-style interface.
Ports-and-adapters boundaries where one domain port is realized over different transports (HTTP, message queue, in-process fake).
Unifying differently shaped data sources (row sets, DTOs, XML or JSON payloads) into one model before they reach domain logic.
Test doubles: an in-memory adapter satisfies the target interface without the real infrastructure.
API wrapper libraries: normalising third-party REST/gRPC APIs (Stripe, Twilio, payment providers) into a stable internal contract so business logic never imports vendor SDK types.
Legacy system integration: wrapping SOAP, CORBA, or mainframe APIs behind a modern interface, enabling incremental migration without rewriting existing clients.
Cloud provider abstraction: a single internal storage or queue interface implemented by AWS, GCP, or Azure adapters, letting the application swap providers via configuration.
ETL pipelines: adapting heterogeneous source record schemas (CSV, JSON, XML, database rows) into one canonical domain record, isolating format changes from downstream consumers.
Event-stream and streaming adapters: translating WebSocket frames or server-sent events into domain events in real time.
Multi-cloud and provider-agnostic interfaces: storage adapters (S3, GCS, Azure Blob), queue adapters (SQS, RabbitMQ, Kafka), and notification adapters that abstract away provider-specific SDKs.
Backend for Frontend (BFF): each front-end client (web, mobile, third-party) gets its own lightweight adapter that shapes internal service responses into the exact payload that client needs.
Java's java.io.InputStreamReader is a byte-to-character bridge: it presents an InputStream through the Reader contract while decoding with an explicit charset.

SLF4J uses providers such as slf4j-reload4j to bind one Logger API to different backends, while log4j-over-slf4j and jul-to-slf4j redirect legacy APIs at a migration boundary; Spring MVC's HandlerAdapter similarly lets DispatcherServlet handle heterogeneous handler types through one SPI.
Go's net/http.HandlerFunc gives an ordinary func(ResponseWriter, *Request) the http.Handler contract by attaching ServeHTTP, so routing and middleware can consume functions and handlers uniformly.
avoid_when: You own both interfaces and can change one cheaply: refactor the contract instead of adding a translation layer that will outlive the mismatch.
The adaptee lacks behaviour the client needs or is functionally wrong: an adapter cannot invent semantics, so change or replace the implementation rather than returning a plausible fake.

The client needs one simplified entry point over several subsystem components: that is Facade, which reshapes a subsystem, not Adapter, which makes one mismatched component satisfy an existing contract.
The target contract should stay unchanged while orthogonal responsibilities such as logging, caching or retries are added: that is Decorator or a higher-order function, not interface translation.
The abstraction and implementation are being designed to vary independently from the outset: that is Bridge; Adapter reconciles an existing mismatch after the two sides already exist.
The mismatch exists at exactly one call site and is not expected to spread: an inline conversion is honest and clearer.
The language's structural typing already gives you the required shape and no isolation or semantic translation is needed: wrapping then only adds indirection.
anti_patterns: God adapter: validation, retries, caching and business rules accumulate until the translation layer becomes a second subsystem instead of a Target-to-Adaptee boundary.
Leaking the adaptee: returning vendor DTOs, exceptions, IDs or the wrapped object lets callers depend on the foreign API again instead of the target contract.
Adapter chains: each layer translates the previous layer, obscuring where semantics changed; consolidate at one boundary or define explicit staged protocols.
Adapter as workaround: wrapping a broken or unstable API postpones the real fix and preserves failure semantics that should be removed; pin, replace or repair it.

Accidental adapter: structural compatibility is mistaken for semantic compatibility, so a type happens to fit while units, errors or lifecycle rules remain wrong; use an explicit contract or no wrapper.
Two-way adapter as indecision: both directions are exposed because nobody chose the domain contract, making ownership and lossiness unclear; choose one Target and make reverse conversion explicit.
Adapter that adds business logic: when translation grows validation, caching, retries or domain rules, it has crossed the boundary; split those concerns into decorators or services.
Capability-gap camouflage: returning plausible defaults for missing adaptee capabilities hides a real gap; fail loudly or expose capability explicitly instead of claiming conformance.
Unversioned adapter registry: dynamic provider resolution without a versioned contract lets a breaking provider change reach callers silently; pin the contract and select deliberately.
design_principles: Program to an interface, not an implementation: the client depends only on Target.
Open/closed: new providers arrive as new adapters while clients and adaptees stay closed for modification.
Single responsibility: interface translation is a responsibility of its own instead of something every call site improvises.
Dependency inversion: high-level policy depends on the abstraction, and the foreign component is reached through it rather than the other way round.
Composition over inheritance: the object adapter that holds its adaptee is preferred over the class adapter.
Information hiding: vendor, legacy and protocol details stop at the adapter's boundary.
Liskov substitution: the adapter must honour Target's full contract, including its error and null semantics.
Leak-tight boundary: vendor types, error codes, ID formats, and protocol details must stop at the adapter; nothing foreign may cross into the domain layer.
Explicit over implicit: every translation — units, nullability, error codes, pagination tokens — must be named and documented rather than assumed from the adaptee's behaviour.
Contract tests over integration tests: verify the adapter against the target interface contract rather than against the live adaptee; contract tests catch interface drift before integration does.
best_practices: Define the target interface from the client's needs first, then write the adapter against it - never mirror the adaptee's API.
Keep adapters thin: translation only, no business logic - if logic creeps in, move it into the domain or the adaptee.
Translate explicitly: units, encodings, parameter order, optionality, error types and timeouts, and document the mapping.
Use the object form by default; choose the inheritance-based class adapter only when the adaptee's protected members or an override point are required.
Name adapters for both sides (for example StripeToPaymentGateway) and keep exactly one adapter per adaptee.
Never return adaptee objects from adapter methods; map into types the target owns.
Test the adapter against the target interface contract (contract tests) rather than testing the SDK.
Adapt once, at the boundary, instead of scattering conversion across call sites.
Keep adapter state thin and lifetime explicit: close or release whatever the adapter owns.
Version adapters independently: when a third-party API changes, create a new adapter version (e.g. StripeV1Adapter, StripeV2Adapter) so existing clients continue working while new ones upgrade.
Encode the full operational contract in the adapter: retries, idempotency keys, exponential backoff, timeouts, and error taxonomies belong to the adapter, not scattered across call sites.
Map external IDs to internal domain identifiers (e.g. UUIDs) so provider-specific ID formats never leak into the domain or appear in domain events and logs.
Use adapter registries or factories for runtime provider selection: the client depends only on the target interface; configuration or a plugin registry picks which concrete adapter to instantiate.
Keep adapters stateless where possible: mutable shared state between adapter instances creates subtle coupling; pass all required context as arguments.
Handle pagination entirely within the adapter using domain-owned cursor types, so provider-specific pagination tokens never surface beyond the adapter boundary.
Document every assumption about the adaptee's error and lifecycle semantics explicitly in the adapter's docstring, especially ownership, timeout behaviour, and which exceptions can propagate.
Combine adapter with decorator for orthogonal concerns (caching, retries, metrics, access logging) while keeping each responsibility in its own class: the adapter translates, the decorator enhances.
Prefer two-way adapters only when both translation directions are used frequently; otherwise keep the direction explicit and single to avoid semantic confusion.
Place adapters in the outer infrastructure layer, never inside domain logic: the domain defines the port in its own language, the adapter lives in infrastructure and translates.
sources: Gamma, Helm, Johnson & Vlissides, Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (1994) - Adapter (Structural Patterns chapter, p. 139); object adapter vs class adapter and their respective trade-offs.

Martin Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (PoEAA), Addison-Wesley, 2002 — Gateway (p. 466) and Mapper (p. 473): Adapter is the GoF ancestor; Gateway encapsulates external system access, Mapper mediates between object representations.
Alur, Crupi & Malks, Core J2EE Patterns: Best Practices and Design Strategies, Prentice Hall, 2nd ed., 2003 — Service Activator, DAO, and Domain Store employ adapter-style boundary translation.

related_patterns_notes.facade: presents a simpler entry point over a subsystem; adapter makes one incompatible component satisfy an existing target contract.
related_patterns_notes.decorator: preserves the target interface while adding responsibilities; adapter changes the adaptee's interface into that target.
related_patterns_notes.proxy: preserves or controls access to a subject with the same interface; adapter intentionally exposes a different interface.
related_patterns_notes.bridge: separates an abstraction from an implementation so both can vary by design; adapter reconciles interfaces that already mismatch.
related_patterns_notes.wrapper-facade: combines wrapping with subsystem simplification; adapter remains focused on one target-to-adaptee translation.
related_patterns_notes.anti-corruption-layer: is a broader domain boundary that protects a model from a foreign system; an adapter may be one implementation inside it.
related_patterns_notes.converter: transforms values or data representations; adapter presents a component under a target behaviour contract and may also translate lifecycle or errors.
related_patterns_notes.delegation: is the forwarding mechanism an adapter can use; it does not by itself define the intent of interface translation.
related_patterns_notes.gateway: names a stable access point to an external system; adapter specifically reconciles that system's incompatible API with a target contract.
related_patterns_notes.mapper: translates object or record shapes; adapter may map data too, but its defining job is substituting a component under a required interface.
